summary: Wilde's friendship with G. H. Kersley across 1885-1894 — 'come and see me' repeated from condolence to reproach for not calling.
certainty_reasoning: The record documents a friendship or acquaintance with no evidence of attraction or romance; classified platonic, upgradable if contrary evidence comes to light.

sources.quote: For the idea of writing simple impressions, I am partly indebted to my noted friend Mr Oscar Wilde, who, I think, agrees with me in only meaning them to appear to the reader short descriptions of any things that have fleeting charms for the poet.
sources.context: Kersley's own words, from the preface to his first book Early Flight (1885), quoted by the editors in their note identifying him. The only place in this record where Kersley speaks. Every other source on this node is Wilde writing to him; this is him writing about Wilde, in public, in the year of the first surviving letter, and claiming him as 'my noted friend'.
sources.speaker: George Herbert Kersley
sources.supports: That the friendship was acknowledged from Kersley's side too, in print.

sources.quote: I am very sorry to hear of your father's death, and hope it will not be any obstacle to your remaining at your work in London. I will come and see you some day and write my name in my book for you, if you tell me when I will find you at home - some afternoon at five - and you will give me a cup of tea, and read me one of your poems. Friday? Would that suit you? I am sure that you will do beautiful work some day. You have the temperament of the artist. Yours sincerely
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [postmark 24 February 1885], 16 Tite Street (MS Rosenbach) - quoted whole, the earliest of the seven. Condolence, an offer to come to him, and a flat statement of belief in him. Wilde was thirty.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: How it started: a death in the family, and Wilde proposing himself for tea.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Kersley, I send you a line for Whitman. I hope you will see him and admire him. Truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [postmark 4 August 1886], Albemarle Club (MS Clark) - quoted whole. Walt Whitman is on this map: Wilde had visited him at Camden in 1882 and the map carries the reported parting kiss. Four years later he is handing a young English poet an introduction to him, and the instruction is not to interview him or learn from him but to 'admire him'. Whether Kersley went is not recorded.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde passing a young poet on to Whitman.

sources.quote: Dear Mr Kersley, I am very pleased that you like my stories. They are studies in prose, put for Romance's sake into a fanciful form: meant partly for children, and partly for those who have kept the childlike faculties of wonder and joy, and who find in simplicity a subtle strangeness. If you come to tea some Wednesday about 5.30 o'clock I will be charmed to write your name in the book. I hope your painting is going on all right. Truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [15 June 1888], 16 Tite Street (F Hyde) - quoted whole. The stories are The Happy Prince and Other Tales, published that May, and the sentence about what they are for is one of the clearest statements Wilde made about them.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The book promised in 1885, three years later, and what Wilde said his stories were for.

sources.quote: My dear Kersley, Of course you should have come to see me before you left town. I wanted to hear all about you, and what art you are now devoted to. As for the art of money-making I know nothing about it. I wish I did, but it is not in my temperament. If I see Charlie Hawtrey I will speak to him about you. Are you writing anything now? Sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [postmark 6 August 1889], 16 Tite Street (MS Clark) - quoted whole. The address has moved from 'Dear Mr Kersley' to 'My dear Kersley'. Charles Hawtrey was an actor-manager; Kersley was after work.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Reproach for not calling, and Wilde offering to put a word in for him.

sources.quote: My dear Kersley, Of course you behaved dreadfully in not coming to see us, but I need hardly tell you you will always be welcome. If you have nothing better to do come in this evening at 9 o'clock or Wednesday afternoons will always find us. It is ages since we met and I want to hear all about you. Truly yours
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [postmark 3 January 1890], 16 Tite Street (TS Clark) - quoted whole. Note the pronoun: 'coming to see US', 'will always find US'. This is the Tite Street household, Wilde and Constance, and the invitation is to it.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The warmest of the invitations, and the reproach repeated five months on.

sources.quote: My dear Kersley, Kleon might do, till we get something better. I dine out tomorrow, but come on Tuesday morning and see me. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [postmark 1 August 1890], 16 Tite Street (MS Clark) - quoted whole; the whole letter is two sentences. 'Kleon' is italicised in the printed text and appears to be a proposed pen-name or title they had been discussing. The sign-off has reached 'Ever yours' and the signature is 'OSCAR' alone.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Two sentences, and both of them are 'come and see me'.

sources.quote: My dear George, I fear that comic footmen do not come into my scheme of art, and the two minor parts of my play - two young dandies - do not come into the possibility of an offer: they are both cast already. But I am cheered to know that you will at any rate be a part of my play, so that I shall have an opportunity of seeing you. You must not think that I have forgotten you: friends who are also poets are never forgotten: memory keeps them in rose-leaves: but Life - coloured, turbulent Life - rushes like a river between oneself and those whom one likes, too often. Sincerely yours
sources.context: Wilde to G. H. Kersley, [postmark 21 November 1894], 16 Tite Street (MS Hyde) - quoted whole, and the last of the seven. Kersley had asked for a part in An Ideal Husband and was given an understudy. Nine years after the first letter the address has reached 'My dear George'. The closing sentence is Wilde apologising for drift, and it is the best writing in the correspondence.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: How Wilde said sorry for losing touch, five months before the trials.
